actions.justification: Patient has HFpEF with decreased urine output, dizziness on standing, and low-normal BP (105/70) — need to determine if volume depleted (over-diuresed) vs. still congested before initiating or adjusting diuretic therapy.

Essential to classify the hemodynamic profile (wet/warm vs. wet/cold) per AHF guidelines. MAP of 82 and HR 95 could suggest borderline perfusion; perfusion assessment will guide whether diuretics, vasodilators, or inotropes are appropriate.

Decreased urine output on hospital day 3 raises concern for cardiorenal syndrome or diuretic-induced AKI. BMP will assess creatinine, BUN, electrolytes (K+, Na+) and guide safe diuretic management per KDIGO AKI workup guidelines.
BNP/NT-proBNP is essential to quantify degree of cardiac decompensation in this HFpEF patient with worsening symptoms on hospital day 3, and will guide treatment intensity.
Chest X-ray will assess for pulmonary edema and degree of congestion, confirming wet status and guiding diuretic therapy in this HFpEF patient with fatigue, dizziness, and decreased urine output.

Patient presents as WET (congested - decreased urine output, worsening fatigue) and WARM (MAP 82, HR 95, SpO2 96%) consistent with volume overload without cardiogenic shock. IV furosemide is the first-line treatment per AHF guidelines for decongestion. Already completed volume/perfusion assessment supports this hemodynamic profile.
Echocardiogram is essential to assess EF, wall motion, diastolic function, and filling pressures in this HFpEF patient. Helps guide further management and confirm diagnosis.
Troponin should be checked to evaluate for acute myocardial injury contributing to decompensated HFpEF, especially given borderline hypotension (BP 105/70) and HR 95.
Cardiology consultation warranted for this complex HFpEF decompensation with borderline hypotension, decreased urine output despite diuresis, and need for optimization of medical therapy.

Patient with HFpEF appears wet and warm (MAP 82, SpO2 96%) with congestion. After IV diuretic initiation, cautious vasodilator therapy (e.g., low-dose nitroglycerin or nitroprusside) can reduce preload/afterload and improve symptoms. BP is borderline (105/70) so careful titration is needed, but MAP of 82 allows cautious use. Inotropes are not indicated in wet/warm profile without cardiogenic shock.

Patient with HFpEF presents with signs of possible low perfusion (BP 105/70, HR 95, decreased urine output, dizziness on standing). While already treated with IV diuretic, the hemodynamic picture with decreased urine output may suggest reduced cardiac output. Inotrope initiation should be considered if cardiogenic shock profile is confirmed (wet and cold), as the only remaining available action in this phase.

Mandatory action not yet completed. Detailed history is essential to characterize the timeline of worsening fatigue, dizziness on standing, and decreased urine output - key symptoms that may indicate diuretic-induced hypovolemia, worsening HFpEF, or AKI in this hospital day 3 patient.

Mandatory action not yet completed. Physical exam is critical to assess volume status (JVP, peripheral edema, lung crackles), perfusion (skin temperature, capillary refill), and hemodynamic profile to guide further management of this HFpEF patient with borderline BP.

Mandatory action not yet completed. ECG is needed to evaluate for arrhythmias (e.g., new atrial fibrillation contributing to decompensation), ischemic changes, or conduction abnormalities in this HFpEF patient with HR 95 and worsening symptoms on hospital day 3.

Mandatory. Patient has decreased urine output on hospital day 3, borderline BP, and is on IV diuretics — BMP is critical to assess renal function, electrolytes (K+, Na+), and guide further diuresis safely.
Mandatory. BNP/NT-proBNP is essential to assess degree of congestion in HFpEF and to guide diuretic titration. This is a distinct mandatory action from the already-completed order_lab_bnp.
Mandatory. CBC needed to evaluate for anemia (which could explain fatigue and dizziness), infection, or other contributing factors in this HFpEF patient.
MANDATORY action - chest X-ray needed to assess for pulmonary edema and degree of congestion in this HFpEF patient with worsening symptoms on hospital day 3.
MANDATORY action - TSH is indicated to rule out thyroid dysfunction as a contributing or exacerbating factor in heart failure with preserved EF and volume overload.

Patient has borderline BP (105/70), decreased urine output, and dizziness on standing suggesting possible shift in hemodynamic profile. Assessing wet/warm vs wet/cold profile guides further management including need for inotropes vs diuretic augmentation.
Assessing LVEF is critical for HFpEF management to confirm preserved EF and guide further treatment decisions. This has not been completed yet per the available actions list.

Patient has decreased urine output on hospital day 3 despite IV furosemide, suggesting diuretic resistance. Adding metolazone (thiazide-like diuretic) provides synergistic diuresis by blocking sodium reabsorption in a different nephron segment, which is a guideline-recommended approach for diuretic resistance in acute heart failure.
Patient remains congested (worsening fatigue, decreased urine output on day 3). Ongoing diuresis optimization is needed to achieve decongestion targets in HFpEF management.

Assessing NYHA functional class is essential for HFpEF management, guiding treatment intensity, device therapy decisions, and establishing baseline for monitoring response to diuresis and other interventions.
